security_hardening.title: Encrypt API keys at rest in database
security_hardening.description: User API keys (Gemini, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Replicate) are stored as plain text in the `user_api_keys` table in `server/src/db/schema.ts`. If the database is compromised, all user API keys are immediately exposed. API keys are high-value secrets that grant access to paid services and could result in significant financial damage if leaked.
security_hardening.rationale: API keys are equivalent to credentials and should be encrypted at rest. A database breach, SQL injection, or insider threat would expose all stored API keys without encryption. Users trust the platform with their sensitive credentials, and plain text storage violates security best practices and compliance requirements.
security_hardening.vulnerability: CWE-312: Cleartext Storage of Sensitive Information
security_hardening.currentRisk: Database compromise exposes all user API keys in plain text, enabling attackers to abuse users' paid AI service accounts
security_hardening.remediation: Implement application-level encryption for API keys before storing in the database. Use AES-256-GCM with a key derived from a secret stored in environment variables or a key management service (GCP Secret Manager). Create encrypt/decrypt utility functions in a new `server/src/lib/crypto.ts` file. Decrypt only when making API calls server-side. Never return decrypted keys to the client.

security_hardening.title: Add explicit HttpOnly and SameSite attributes to session cookies
security_hardening.description: The Lucia session cookie configuration in `server/src/lib/auth.ts` only sets the `secure` attribute for production. The `httpOnly` and `sameSite` attributes are not explicitly configured, relying on Lucia defaults that may vary. Explicit configuration ensures consistent session security across all environments.
security_hardening.rationale: HttpOnly prevents JavaScript access to cookies, mitigating XSS-based session theft. SameSite=Lax or Strict prevents CSRF attacks by ensuring cookies are not sent in cross-origin requests. While Lucia likely sets reasonable defaults, explicit configuration ensures predictable security behavior and makes security audits clearer.
security_hardening.currentRisk: XSS vulnerabilities could lead to session hijacking if cookies are accessible to JavaScript. Cross-site request forgery may be possible without explicit SameSite restriction.
security_hardening.remediation: Update Lucia configuration to explicitly set: `sessionCookie: { attributes: { secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production', httpOnly: true, sameSite: 'lax' } }`. Consider 'strict' for sameSite if cross-site navigation with auth isn't required.

security_hardening.title: Add rate limiting to public sharing endpoints
security_hardening.description: The public sharing routes (`/api/sharing/public/*`) in `server/src/routes/sharing.ts` lack rate limiting, making them vulnerable to brute force attacks on share tokens, comment spam on shared designs, and enumeration attacks. Unlike auth and AI endpoints which have rate limiting, these public routes have no protection.
security_hardening.rationale: Share tokens (UUIDs) are the only authorization mechanism for accessing shared content. While UUIDs are hard to guess, systematic requests can enumerate valid tokens over time. Comment endpoints without rate limits enable spam flooding that degrades user experience.
security_hardening.vulnerability: CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts
security_hardening.currentRisk: Unlimited requests to public sharing endpoints allow brute force attacks on share tokens, comment spam flooding, and resource exhaustion. No monitoring of suspicious access patterns.
security_hardening.remediation: 1. Apply rate limiting middleware to all `/api/sharing/public/*` routes. 2. Suggested limits: 30 requests/minute for design access (GET), 10 comments/minute per IP (POST). 3. Add `publicRateLimit` and `commentRateLimit` to rateLimit.ts. 4. Consider CAPTCHA for comment submission. 5. Log rate limit violations to detect attacks.

security_hardening.title: Implement input sanitization for comment content
security_hardening.description: The comment creation endpoint in `server/src/routes/sharing.ts` (lines 79-115) accepts `content` and `author_name` directly from user input without sanitization or validation. While React escapes output by default, stored XSS could occur if this data is rendered in non-React contexts (emails, PDF exports, admin panels, future integrations).
security_hardening.rationale: Defense in depth requires sanitizing user input at the storage layer, not just relying on output encoding. Malicious payloads stored in the database persist and affect all viewers. Content could be rendered in multiple contexts where XSS protection varies.
security_hardening.vulnerability: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (Stored XSS)
security_hardening.currentRisk: Malicious JavaScript in comments could execute in admin dashboards, email notifications, or future integrations that don't properly escape output. No content length limits enable DoS via oversized comments.
security_hardening.remediation: 1. Add server-side sanitization using a library like `sanitize-html` or `xss`. 2. Strip HTML tags from comment content. 3. Limit content length (e.g., max 2000 characters). 4. Validate author_name against an allowlist of characters (alphanumeric + spaces). 5. Add validation helper: `const sanitizeComment = (content: string) => content.slice(0, 2000).replace(/<[^>]*>/g, '');`

security_hardening.title: Implement email verification status tracking and enforcement
security_hardening.description: The authentication system generates and sends email verification tokens but never actually marks users as verified. The `users` table in `server/src/db/schema.ts` lacks an `email_verified` column, and the verify-email endpoint in `server/src/routes/auth.ts` only deletes the token without updating user status. No routes enforce verification before allowing access to sensitive features.
security_hardening.rationale: Email verification ensures users control the email address they register with, preventing account squatting and enabling secure password recovery. Without tracking verification status, malicious users could register with others' email addresses and gain trust. This is explicitly noted as a TODO in the codebase (auth.ts line 239-241).
security_hardening.currentRisk: Users can operate accounts with unverified email addresses, potentially impersonating others. Password recovery could send reset links to attacker-controlled addresses if email ownership isn't verified. No audit trail of verified vs unverified users.
security_hardening.remediation: 1) Add `emailVerified: boolean('email_verified').default(false)` to the users schema. 2) Update the verify-email endpoint to: `await db.update(users).set({ emailVerified: true }).where(eq(users.id, token.userId));` 3) Add middleware to restrict certain actions (API key management, sharing, team invites) to verified users only. 4) Consider sending re-verification emails when email is changed.

positiveFindings: No known CVEs in npm dependencies (frontend: 0 vulnerabilities, backend: 0 vulnerabilities)
CSRF protection enabled via hono/csrf middleware
Comprehensive security headers (HSTS 2-year with preload, CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy)
Password hashing uses Argon2 with OWASP-recommended parameters (memoryCost: 19456, timeCost: 2, outputLen: 32)
Strong password policy enforced (8+ chars, uppercase, lowercase, number, special character required)
Account lockout after 5 failed login attempts with 15-minute lockout period
Password reset tokens are SHA-256 hashed before storage (plain token sent in email only)
API keys are masked in client responses (only last 4 characters shown via maskKey helper)
Rate limiting on authentication endpoints (5/min login, 3/min signup, 3/min forgot-password, 5/min reset-password)
Rate limiting on AI endpoints (30 requests/minute global)
User enumeration prevented on login and forgot-password endpoints (generic error messages)
No eval/exec/system patterns detected in server codebase
Drizzle ORM uses parameterized queries - no SQL injection via string concatenation
Session cookies set with secure flag in production mode
CORS properly configured with explicit origin allowlist (no wildcard)
Authorization checks on storage routes verify user owns requested file path
Admin routes require both authentication and admin role verification with granular permissions
Admin audit logging tracks all sensitive administrative operations
